detail: The bridge crosses the main arm of the Seine, connecting the quai de Gesvres to the quai de la Corse on the Île de la Cité. It stands on the site of one of the earliest bridges in Paris, the Grand-Pont, which was later replaced by the planches de Milbray. That structure was followed by two successive versions called the pont Notre-Dame, the first built in wood and the second in stone. The modern bridge measures 105 metres in length and 20 metres in width, with a central metal arch spanning 60 metres.

Although few kings actually stayed there for long periods, the hôtel des Tournelles served for many years as a residence for the monarchs of France. Following the death of Henri II, the king's widow, Catherine de' Medici, abandoned the palace because she considered it outdated. Before being sold off to fund the construction of an Italian-style palace, the Tuileries, the building was temporarily converted into a powder magazine.

Built on the Right Bank during the Hundred Years' War, the royal residence took its name from the parish church of Saint-Paul-des-Champs. Although located outside the wall of Philip Augustus, it was protected by the fort and bastide Saint-Anthoine-lez-Paris, built between 1356 and 1358, and by the wall of Charles V, also begun in 1356. Only Charles V and Charles VI held court here. Following the death of Charles VI in 1422, the royal family abandoned the complex for the hôtel des Tournelles and the Louvre. Charles VII and Louis XI granted portions of the estate to loyal supporters, before it was systematically broken up under François I and Henri III.

From the 9th century, access to the two bridges linking the Île de la Cité to the riverbanks was defended by two fortresses, constructed first in wood and later rebuilt in stone. The southern fortress, situated at the far end of the Petit-Pont, was named the Petit Châtelet to distinguish it from the Grand Châtelet across the Grand Pont (now the pont au Change). In local usage, when the name Châtelet is mentioned on its own in Paris, it refers specifically to the Grand Châtelet.

A section of the palace was converted into a state prison in 1370 after Charles V and his successors abandoned it as a royal residence. The Conciergerie prison occupied the ground floor of the building along the quai de l'Horloge and its two towers, while the upper floor was reserved for the Parlement de Paris. During the Terror, it held defendants awaiting trial before the Revolutionary Tribunal between 1793 and 1795, including Queen Marie-Antoinette in 1793. A large portion of the historical site continued to house the law courts of Paris until the spring of 2018.

Created on 25 June 864 under King Charles II through the Edict of Pîtres, the Monnaie de Paris is the national minting institution of France. It is one of the oldest operating companies in the world and the oldest surviving French institution. Responsible for producing the nation's coinage, it functioned for centuries under direct government oversight as part of the Ministry of Economy, Finance and Industry. It gained full administrative autonomy and legal status as a public industrial and commercial establishment under a 2007 finance law.

The name is sometimes misspelled as Fort l'Évêque. The facility served as the prison for the bishops of Paris from 1222 until 1674, after which it functioned as one of the royal prisons from 1674 to 1780, shortly before its demolition in 1783.

The hôtel d'Alençon adjoined the hôtel du Petit-Bourbon, which stood opposite the drawbridge of the east gate of the medieval Louvre. The site lay between the fossé Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois, now the southern section of the rue de l'Amiral-de-Coligny, and the former rue d'Autriche, bounded on one side by the Right Bank of the Seine.

Built at the end of the 14th century for the Duke of Bourbon, the residence stood between the fossé Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois (the southern portion of modern rue de l'Amiral-de-Coligny) and the former rue d'Autriche, adjoining the hôtel d'Alençon and the Right Bank of the Seine. The north wing housed a gallery known as the salle or théâtre du Petit-Bourbon, which served as a venue for royal festivities, ballets, and theatrical performances. The actors Molière and Scaramouche both performed in the hall with their respective theatre troupes before its destruction.

Originally built outside the city wall of Philip Augustus in 1190, the fortress became the primary residence of French monarchs under Charles V in the 14th century, holding the royal library and the Treasury. Over an 800-year construction history, the medieval castle and its keep were gradually demolished. Henri IV later linked the Louvre to Catherine de' Medici's Tuileries Palace by building the Grande Galerie along the Seine, and Louis XIV added the monumental east colonnade to the Cour Carrée. Besides the main museum, the palace today houses the Musée des Arts Décoratifs and the École du Louvre.

Constructed at the beginning of the 13th century, the Tour de Nesle formed one of the corner towers of the city wall built by Philip Augustus. The vanished tower stood at the exact site now occupied by the eastern pavilion of the Institut de France. It was described historically as unquestionably the most famous of all the towers in old Paris.

The church originally developed from a 7th-century chapel in the cemetery of Saint-Martial, a women's monastery on the Île de la Cité. Located at numbers 30–32 rue Saint-Paul, it served as the royal parish due to its proximity to both the hôtel Saint-Paul and the hôtel des Tournelles. Following its demolition, a new parish was established in the early 19th century and assigned to the former professed house of the Jesuits, the église Saint-Louis-des-Jésuites, which was then renamed Saint-Paul-Saint-Louis.

Commonly called the Hôtel de Ville, this building has housed the municipal institutions of Paris since 1357. Because Paris has experienced various insurrections throughout its history, the municipal building frequently became a rallying point for rioters, insurgents, and revolutionaries. It stands as a location deeply marked by history, witnessing moments from the time of Étienne Marcel to the Fronde, from the French Revolution to the revolutionary days of July 1830 and February 1848, and from the Commune to the Liberation of Paris. After being totally burned down at the end of the Paris Commune, it was rebuilt identically in the following years.

Known as the ancestor of the modern Cour des comptes, the Chambre des comptes of Paris was the oldest of all the accounting courts in France after the Exchequer of Normandy. Under the Ancien Régime, these chambers operated as sovereign courts specifically dedicated to handling financial affairs.

The full name of this now-vanished monastery was the couvent des Cordelières de l'église de Sainte-Claire à l'Ourcine-lèz-Saint-Marcel (près de Paris). Founded in 1289 by Gallien de Poix at the gates of Paris in the faubourg Saint-Marcel, it was established at the request of Marguerite de Provence. Following its destruction, the rue de Julienne, rue Pascal, and rue des Cordelières were created across the site of its former enclosure.

This former Parisian church was also known as the prieuré, monastère, or église Sainte-Catherine-de-la-Couture. Established by the sergeants-at-arms of the king's guard in memory of the Battle of Bouvines, the religious complex was destroyed at the end of the eighteenth century. Its outbuildings and grounds were used as a cemetery.

Before becoming the chief house of the Hospitallers of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem following the transfer of Templar property, the priory was the largest Templar commandery in France. Until the Revolution, the enclosure retained the status of a bailiwick within Paris. This status gave the area tax exemption, made it exempt from guild regulations, and allowed it to serve as a place of refuge for insolvent debtors. Known today as the enclos du Temple, the site gave its name to the surrounding district.

Its founder, William of Champeaux, served as archdeacon and schoolmaster of the cathedral school of Notre-Dame. The intellectual influence of the abbey grew through famous masters such as Hugh, Adam, Andrew, Richard, and Thomas Gallus. Following its suppression in 1790 and demolition in 1811, the site was initially occupied by the wine market (halle aux vins). In the second half of the 20th century it was replaced by the science faculty, and it now houses the Institut de physique du globe alongside the Jussieu campus. The abbey's motto was Jesus, Maria, sanctus Victor, sanctus Augustinus.

Saint Médéric, after whom the church is named, died in the year 700, and his remains rest in the crypt. Located on the rue Saint-Martin along the line of the old Roman north-south road, Saint-Merri is regarded as one of the four daughters of Notre-Dame cathedral. Its architectural similarity to Notre-Dame earned it the nickname Notre-Dame la petite. Although built between 1500 and 1565 during the Renaissance, it remains Flamboyant Gothic in style. Today it holds a prestigious organ and a collection of 17th- and 19th-century paintings.

Also known as the Collège Saint-Bernard, the institution was founded at 20 rue de Poissy by Stephen of Lexington, abbot of Clairvaux, with the encouragement of Pope Innocent IV. The college's church was largely destroyed by the laying out of the rue de Pontoise, and its remaining ruins were cleared in 1859 during the creation of the boulevard Saint-Germain. Designated a historical monument in 1887, the complex underwent a complete renovation that finished in September 2008. Since 2009, it has housed the Académie catholique de France.

Construction began in 1491 with the choir and bell tower to serve the parish surrounding Sainte-Geneviève abbey, concluding with the façade in 1624. Briefly converted into a Temple of Filial Piety during the French Revolution, the building returned to parish use in 1801. It retains the shrine of Saint Genevieve, though its relics were lost during the Revolution, as well as an organ case dating back to the 1630s. Saint-Étienne-du-Mont is notably the last church in Paris that still preserves a rood screen (jubé).

The church stands within the former enclos Saint-Laurent in the 10th arrondissement. The ancient Roman north-south highway on which it was built connected Senlis and Orléans, laid out in the middle of the first century BC along the line of the modern rue Saint-Martin and rue Saint-Jacques. Following initial historical protections granted in 1945, Saint-Laurent was fully classified as a monument historique in 2016.

Founded to replace a late sixth-century basilica destroyed by the Normans, the monastery held a privileged enclosure hosting an annual fair. Supported by royal patronage, the priory eventually controlled around thirty dependencies across ten dioceses, extending into England. Its choir, built between roughly 1135 and 1155, combines Romanesque design with early Gothic elements and provided an early prototype for ambulatories with radiating chapels. The surviving refectory, constructed between 1225 and 1235, is considered a masterpiece of Rayonnant Gothic architecture.

Construction lasted nearly two centuries, finishing around 1345. Seat of the Archdiocese of Paris, the cathedral combines features of early and Rayonnant Gothic architecture, featuring two transept rose windows that rank among the largest in Europe. Between 1845 and 1867, architect Eugène Viollet-le-Duc directed a major restoration, adding new elements including a spire. Serving as a royal parish church in the Middle Ages, Notre-Dame received the Crown of Thorns in 1239. It later hosted the coronation of Napoleon I in 1804, the baptism of the last Bourbon of France in 1821, and the state funerals of several French presidents.

Te hospital originally functioned as a hostelry for pilgrims travelling to holy sites like Jerusalem or Santiago de Compostela. For centuries it was run by Augustinian nuns with nursing skills, while doctors only began practising inside hospitals during the 18th century. Before then, physicians treated wealthy paying patients at home, leaving poor and indigent patients to receive free care in hospitals.

The leper house was originally run by a religious community. The vast enclosure was bounded on the south by the rue de Paradis, on the east by the rue du Faubourg-Saint-Denis, on the north by the boulevard de la Chapelle, and on the west by the rue du Faubourg-Poissonnière. It also covered parts of the former 3rd and 5th arrondissements. The recorded history of Saint-Lazare contains many gaps, as its archives were destroyed in succession during the Hundred Years' War, throughout the Wars of Religion, and during the looting of the site on 13 July 1789.

The cemetery took its name from the church of the Saints-Innocents, which stood at the north-east corner of the square and is today gone. The church was dedicated to the Holy Innocents, the children of Judea massacred by order of King Herod. The cemetery itself possessed up to two reclusories, which were the most famous of all those in Paris.

The chapel was built on the Île de la Cité on the site of the former chapel of Saint-Nicolas-du-Palais. Designed as the first of the 'saintes chapelles', it was conceived as a vast reliquary, almost entirely glazed, and constructed in no more than seven years. In addition to the Crown of Thorns, it was built to house a fragment of the True Cross. A college of canons served the chapel until 1787. Closed for worship around 1790, it was emptied of its contents and used as the headquarters of the Club de la Sainte-Chapelle. In 1797 it became an archives store for the Palais de Justice, whose expansion threatened its survival.

The convent was located at the site of present-day 158 rue Saint-Jacques. The name Jacobins derived from Saint-Jacques, as Jacques is Jacobus in Latin. Its teaching activity formed the Collège des Jacobins, a college within the former University of Paris. Suppressed in 1790 during the French Revolution, the convent buildings were demolished between 1800 and 1849. In 1849, Father Lacordaire re-established the Dominicans of the Saint-Jacques convent at a new site, located today at 20 rue des Tanneries in the 13th arrondissement.

The Filles-Dieu were a French religious congregation of hospital nuns. Around the year 1300, they had first been known as the Sœurs de Saint-Gervais because they were put in charge of servicing the hospital of that name. The sisters wore a habit consisting of a white dress underneath a black cloak. Beyond their foundation in Paris, the order held its principal houses in Orléans, Beauvais, and Abbeville.

During the French Revolution, the former convent served as the headquarters for the Cordeliers Club of Danton and Desmoulins. Under the First Empire, the site became the headquarters of the École pratique of the Paris faculty of medicine. The surviving refectory was restored by the Régie immobilière de la ville de Paris.

The order was founded following the sermons of Jean Tisserand, a Cordelier preacher at Notre-Dame de Paris. Before moving in 1572, the convent was installed in the Hôtel d'Orléans, on the site now occupied by the Bourse de Commerce. Popularly nicknamed the Filles de Paris, the nuns were later known as the Augustines of the Order of Penance of Mary Magdalene. They remained in the buildings of the abbey of Saint-Magloire on the rue Saint-Denis until the community was suppressed in 1790.

Saint-Séverin has been the seat of a parish since the ninth century. At the time of the confiscation of church property in 1789, it was one of fifty-two urban parishes in the diocese of Paris, and its parish priest held office as one of the two archpriests of the diocese. Today, the church, its presbytery and parish house, the cloister, and square André-Lefèbvre form an ensemble bounded by rue des Prêtres-Saint-Séverin, rue de la Parcheminerie, rue Saint-Jacques, and rue Saint-Séverin.

First founded under the name of Sainte-Croix et Saint-Vincent, the abbey church was consecrated on 23 April 558. The original basilica featured marble columns, a paneled ceiling, and glass windows, and served as a royal burial site until the creation of the royal necropolis at Saint-Denis. As a royal abbey, it enjoyed special exemptions and was directly subject to the Pope.

The church was rebuilt from the end of the tenth century under Abbot Morard. The nave, transept, and lower four levels of the western bell tower date from this period. In the mid-twelfth century, a new choir was built in the early Gothic style and consecrated by Pope Alexander III on 21 April 1163, making it one of the earliest Gothic structures.

The founder, Cardinal Lemoine (1250–1313), died in Avignon. He had been sent to Paris by the pope as a legate with the mission of ending hostilities between France and England. Established in the fourteenth century, the institution functioned as a college attached to the University of Paris.

To establish the institution, Joan of Navarre, wife of Philip the Fair, bequeathed her townhouse on the rue Saint-André-des-Arts. This bequest served to found the educational institution of the old University of Paris on the rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Geneviève, which was designed to receive students from her own kingdom.

In 1317, a bequest from a Breton cleric provided for five scholarships. In 1374, Canon Jean de Guestry—a master of arts and medicine and physician to the king—bought a house on the rue du Plâtre for the scholars and added five more scholarships. The statutes of the college were approved at its opening by Maignac, Bishop of Paris. The institution was eventually merged into the collège Louis-le-Grand in 1763.

Tracing its origin back to the twelfth century, the faculty was one of the four main faculties of the old University of Paris. In 1679, it became the faculty of civil and canon law. Following its closure during the French Revolution in 1793, it was refounded in 1802 and became the new law faculty of Paris in 1808. The historic building constructed in 1771 on the place du Panthéon to house it is today shared between the universities of Paris I and Paris II.

As one of the foreign colleges of the old university, it was established at the instigation of André Ghini—bishop of Arras and later Tournai—alongside three other Italian benefactors to endow scholarships for eleven needy scholars, sons of Lombards (Italians). Situated on the rue Saint-Hilaire (now rue des Carmes), the house was officially named the Maison des Pauvres Écoliers italiens de la Charité de la Bienheureuse Marie. It declined in the seventeenth century.

The founder, Nicolas Coqueret, was a priest from Amiens. Situated in the courtyard of the former hôtel de Bourgogne, the site lay between today's rue de Lanneau, rue d'Écosse, and impasse Chartière. Geoffroy Tory served as regent in 1530, and the college was famous for its courses in astronomy and medicine. By abandoning the scholastic jargon of Thomist and Aristotelian philosophy, the institution provoked disputes that resulted in its closure during the troubles of the Catholic League. Other notable students included Jean Antoine de Baïf, Rémy Belleau, Pierre Bunel, and Domingo de Soto.

The college was situated at No. 115 rue Saint-Jacques, to the right of the collège Louis-le-Grand and next to the collège de Marmoutiers. Following the demolition of its buildings in 1864, the northern section of the modern Lycée Louis-le-Grand was built on its site, forming the present cours Molière.

The college received income from the priory of Notre-Dame de Marceille in Limoux until the eighteenth century. Its former student Pierre Roger, later Pope Clement VI, subsequently funded the institution. It had sixteen bursars in 1544, but later declined; when it was merged into the collège Louis-le-Grand in 1763, only one bursar remained. In 1481, a book titled La Confession by Olivier Maillard was printed at the college; the Musée Condé in Chantilly holds a copy, and no other works are known to have been produced by its press.

Also known as the domus de Sorbonna, the college occupied buildings on the site of the modern Sorbonne on the rue des Écoles. During the Renaissance, its faculty of theology was mocked for its conservatism by François Rabelais, who dubbed them Sorbonnagres ('the asses of the Sorbonne'). The institution was suppressed in 1793 when the National Convention closed all universities in France. Its name survives today in four Parisian universities: Sorbonne Université, Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, Sorbonne-Nouvelle, and Sorbonne-Paris-Nord.

The site of the college extended in the fifth arrondissement from the southern side of the place de la Sorbonne to the rue Cujas, and from the rue Victor-Cousin towards the boulevard Saint-Michel. Today, a portion of this site is occupied by the Hôtel des 3 Collèges.

The rampart of Charles V was one of seven major city walls built around Paris over time, replacing the wall of Philip Augustus on the Right Bank. Its western section was demolished around 1640 after becoming unnecessary following the construction of the Louis XIII wall. Its eastern fortifications were reinforced with bastions in the mid-sixteenth century before being destroyed from 1670 onwards, giving way to the Grands Boulevards. Few traces remain, but the wall left a strong mark on the city's plan.

There were two successive gates bearing this name at different locations along the rue Saint-Antoine in the modern fourth arrondissement. The first dated from the very beginning of the thirteenth century. The second, built in the mid-fourteenth century, was the more famous gate, protected by the fortress of the Bastille.

Formerly known as the fort et bastide Saint-Anthoine lez Paris, the fortress was built where the rue Saint-Antoine opens onto the present-day place de la Bastille. After becoming a prison and being viewed as a symbol of monarchical despotism, it was completely destroyed at the start of the French Revolution.

The bastion formed part of the eastern fortifications of the wall of Charles V (1356–1383), which replaced the wall of Philip Augustus on the Right Bank. The eastern section of the rampart was strengthened with bastions in the mid-sixteenth century and was destroyed starting in 1670, making way for the Grands Boulevards.

The replacement gate was erected in 1674 by order of Louis XIV to celebrate his victories on the Rhine and in Franche-Comté. Designed by the architect Pierre Bullet—a pupil of François Blondel, who built the nearby Porte Saint-Denis—it stands where the adjacent walls were later destroyed. The monument was listed as a historic monument in 1862, and restoration work was carried out in 1988.

Also recorded under the spelling Bussy, the gate was one of two known as the portes Saint-Germain. Situated in today's Saint-Germain-des-Prés quarter near the carrefour de l'Odéon, it was destroyed along with the rest of the wall of Philip Augustus in the seventeenth century.

Originally called the porte des Cordeliers before being renamed porte Saint-Germain, this was one of two gates serving the area alongside the porte de Buci. Built in the thirteenth century on the wall of Philip Augustus near the carrefour de l'Odéon in today's Saint-Germain-des-Prés quarter, it was destroyed in the seventeenth century.

Also known as the collège de Dormans-Beauvais, this college of the former University of Paris became a major centre of Jansenism in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries. During this period, it was widely attended by the children of parliamentarians. Situated in the fifth arrondissement, the surviving college building is officially classified as a historic monument.

The gates built along the rue Montmartre are not to be confused with the modern Porte de Montmartre. Over time, three successive gates stood along this route to accommodate the outward expansion of the city's fortifications. Each gate was demolished in turn to ease traffic movement and improve the supply of provisions into Paris.

It served as the main western entrance to Paris towards Saint-Germain-en-Laye, forming a cardinal entry point alongside the Porte Saint-Denis to the north heading to Saint-Denis, the Porte Saint-Antoine to the east towards Vincennes, and the Porte Saint-Jacques to the south towards Orléans. Like other gates along the rue Saint-Honoré, each successive structure was eventually demolished to improve traffic flow and ease the supply of goods into the city.

The river flows for 774.76 kilometres across the Paris Basin, rising at an altitude of 446 metres at Source-Seine in Côte-d'Or on the Langres plateau. Following a general course from south-east to north-west, it passes through Troyes, Paris, Rouen, and Le Havre before emptying into the English Channel between Le Havre and Honfleur. Its drainage basin covers 79,000 square kilometres.

The island was also known historically as the île aux Javiaux and the île d'Antragues, and fell under the administrative quarter of the Cité before being attached to the riverbank in the 19th century. According to Michel Roblin, it was called the île aux meules because of its proximity to the port au Foin hay market. The historian Jacques-Antoine Dulaure noted several additional variant names for the island, including île des Meules-aux-Javeaux, île Bouteclou, and île-aux-Ourmetiaux.

The tapestry workshop was established in April 1601 under Henri IV, acting on the advice of his commerce advisor Barthélemy de Laffemas. Officially named the Manufacture nationale des Gobelins and located in the 13th arrondissement, its gallery was renovated starting in the late 1970s and reopened to the public on 12 May 2007 to mark its 400th anniversary. The complex and its grounds are classified as historical monuments.

Though built outside the city walls, the fair was gradually integrated into the urban fabric of Paris. It played a major commercial role with over 120 stalls, known as 'loges'. From the 17th century it hosted fairground shows, which expanded significantly during the 18th century before shifting to the boulevard theatres. The 15th-century fair buildings were destroyed by fire in 1762 and partially rebuilt in 1762–1763, before being demolished in 1811 to create the Marché Saint-Germain.

The western section between the rue des Barres and the rue de Fourcy was renamed rue François-Miron by a decree of 2 October 1865. In 1227, the stretch running from the rue des Barres to the rue de la Culture Sainte-Catherine (now the rue de Sévigné) was known as the rue de l'Aigle and the rue de la porte Baudeer (also written Baudoyer or Baudet). Beyond that point, the continuation of the street was known as the rue du Pont Perrin.

The street is recorded as existing in 1358, appearing in early documents under spelling variants such as Pute y Musse, Pute y Muce, Petit Musse, and Petit Muce before taking the form Petit-Musc. In 1532, the historian Corrozet recorded it under the name rue de la Petite Pusse, while several 16th-century maps designated it as the rue des Célestins.

Originally known as the rue du Comte de Boulogne, the street was later recorded by Sauval under the name rue Richebourg. In 1713, the section between the rue des Fossés Saint-Marcel and the rue du Pont aux Biches (now the rue de la Clef) was called the rue des Morts, while the remaining stretch was named the rue Permoulin. The rue des Morts later became the rue de la Muette and the rue Permoulin became the rue du Fer à Moulin, before both sections were unified in 1806 under the single name Fer à Moulin.

The former rue de Lourcine appeared under numerous spelling variants over time, including Loursine, l'Oursine, l'Orsine, l'Ursine, and Lorcines. It was also referred to as the rue du Clos Ganay and the rue de la Franchise, while the cartographer Dheulland recorded it as the rue des Cordelières. In 1938, the section between the rue Mouffetard and the rue Claude Bernard was renamed rue Edouard Quénu, and in 1944 the stretch between boulevard Arago and rue de la Santé became rue Léon-Maurice Nordmann.

In addition to rue de la Culture Sainte-Catherine, the thoroughfare was historically recorded as the rue de la Couture Sainte-Catherine. The section lying between the rue des Francs Bourgeois and the rue du Parc Royal was reportedly once known as the rue du Val.

The street appears as the rue Perciée on the tax roll of 1313. Later sources distinguished it from other streets of the same name: the historian La Tynna recorded it as the rue Percée Saint-Paul in 1816, while Felix Lazare listed it as the rue Percée Saint-Antoine in 1844 before it was renamed.

Opened at the beginning of the 13th century, the street was originally named the rue des Bouliers (or au Bouloir) and the rue de Richebourg. Over time it was also known as the rue Neuve d'Orléans and simply the rue d'Orléans, before being designated as the rue d'Orléans Saint-Marcel.

Opened at the end of the 13th century, the street originally formed part of the rue Neuve-du-Temple, also known as the rue du Chantier du Temple. It initially extended as far as the rue Portefoin before being divided into the rue du Grand Chantier and the rue des Enfants Rouges. It was later merged alongside several adjoining historic streets to form the modern rue des Archives.

In 1300, Guillot listed the street simply as the rue du Temple. Over time it accumulated various titles, including rue de la Culture du Temple, rue de la Clôture du Temple, rue de l'Egout du Temple, rue de la Poterne Barbette, and rue Vieille Barbette. The street originally began at the rue Saint-Antoine (now rue François-Miron); the section between that street and the rue de Rivoli was joined to the rue du Pont Louis-Philippe by a decree of 13 July 1885.

The street bore several early variations of its name, including rue des Viez Poulies, Vieilles Poulies, Richard des Poulies, and Ferri des Poulies. During the French Revolution, it was temporarily renamed rue des Francs Citoyens. By a decree of 2 April 1868, the rue des Francs-Bourgeois absorbed the rue Neuve Sainte-Catherine and the rue de Paradis au Marais (known in 1787 as the rue des Jardins), followed on 26 December 1893 by a section of the rue des Vosges.

Over its long history, the street carried a wide variety of names, including rue de la Culture du Temple, rue de la Couture du Temple, rue de la Clôture du Temple, and rue de l'Egout du Temple. It was also known as rue de la Porte Barbette, rue de la Poterne Barbette, rue Barbette, and rue Vieille Barbette. The rue Vieille du Temple formerly began at the rue Saint-Antoine (the modern rue François Miron). A decree on 13 July 1885 united the section between that street and the rue de Rivoli with the rue du Pont Louis-Philippe.

The rue des Rosiers formerly ran between the rue des Juifs (now the rue Ferdinand-Duval) and the rue Vieille du Temple. The present street also includes the former impasse Coquerelle, which extended for a length of 47 metres from the rue des Juifs in line with the rue des Rosiers. This impasse originated from a street that was originally named the rue de la Lamproie, before being recorded under the names Coquerée in 1415 and Coquerrie in 1540.

Before the creation of the rue de Rivoli, the northern section of the street was included in the rue Tiron. The main body of the street was known as the rue de l'Ecofle in 1233, de l'Escoufle in 1300, des Escoufles in 1313, and des Escofles in 1430, before taking the names des Esclosses and finally des Ecouffes. In March 2017, a municipal decision designated the section of the street running between the rue de Rivoli and the rue du Roi de Sicile as the passage Walter Benjamin.

Before taking its present name, this street was known as the rue des Juifs, and earlier still as the rue des Rosiers. It appears to have existed as early as the 13th century. Following a municipal decision passed on 11, 12, 13, and 14 June 2019, the section of the street running between the rue de Rivoli and the rue du Roi de Sicile, which had incorporated the former passage du Petit Saint-Antoine, was named rue Pierre Seel.

By an order of 2 April 1868, the rue de Bercy Saint-Jean was united with the rue du Roi de Sicile. That street had previously been known as the rue de Bercy or rue de Bercy au Marais. In the 14th century it was called rue du Hoqueton, Hoqueton le Faucheur, or rue Bouquetonne, before later taking the names rue de la Réale and rue de Berci. A section between the rue Vieille du Temple and the rue du Bourg Tibourg, known as the rue de la Croix Blanche in the early 15th century, had many earlier names in the 13th century, including rue Augustin Lefaucheur, Anquetin le Faucheur, and Hennequin le Faucheur. During the French Revolution, it was called the rue des Droits de l'Homme. The rue du Roi de Sicile itself existed by the middle of the 13th century.

Before taking its present designation, the street was formed from the rue de l'Etoile and the rue du Fauconnier. The former rue de l'Etoile was known over time by numerous names, including rue des Barrés, des Petites Barrières, Petite Barrée, Tillebarrée, Tête Barrée, de l'Arche Dorée, and de l'Arche Beaufils. The historic rue du Fauconnier was also referred to as the rue des Fauconniers or rue Fauconnière, and appears under the name rue Ragonni on the Tapestry map (plan de la Tapisserie).

The street formed part of an ancient Gallo-Roman road running from Lutetia to Fontainebleau. In the 13th century, it was an old path traversing a territory called Mont Cetarius or Certadus. The road was designated by a wide variety of names, including Montfétard, Maufetard, Mofetard, Moufetard, Mouflard, Moftard, and Mostard. It was also called the rue Saint-Marcel, rue du Faubourg Saint-Marceau, and rue de la Vieille Ville Saint-Marcel. Parts of the original thoroughfare were later absorbed by the avenue des Gobelins and the rue de Bazeilles.

The present rue Volta was formed from three distinct sections. The first, the rue Frépillon, ran between the rue au Maire and the old rue Phélipeaux; it existed by 1269 and was variously written Ferpillon, Ferpeillon, Fripilon, or Serpillon. The middle section was the rue de la Croix or de la Croix Neuve, dating from the 14th century, between the rue Phélipeaux and the rue du Vertbois. The northern section, the rue du Pont aux Biches (or rue du Pont aux Biches Saint-Martin), ran between the rue du Vertbois and Notre-Dame de Nazareth and appears on the Braun map of 1530.

The rue du Temple consolidated several historic streets. The southernmost section, the rue des Coquilles, was called ruelle Gentien, ruelle Jean Gentien, and rue Jacques Gentien in the 14th century. The rue Barre du Bec, running between the rue de la Verrerie and the rue Saint-Merri, was named rue de l'Abbéie du Bec Hellouin by Guillot in 1300. Further north, the rue Sainte-Avoie was called the grande rue du Temple, and by 1515 was known interchangeably as rue du Temple or rue Sainte-Avoie. Beyond the rue Michel le Comte, the street was recorded in 1235 as vicus Militiæ Templi (or rue de la Milice du Temple) and in 1252 as rue de la Chevalerie du Temple.

The section of the street running between the rue Saint-Martin and the rue Beaubourg was called rue du Seigneur de Montmorency from the 14th century. The eastern section between the rue Beaubourg and the rue du Temple, recorded in 1328 as the ruelle au Villain, was later known as rue Cour au Villain. The mapmaker Lacaille wrote it as rue Courtauvillain or ruelle Auvillain. This eastern stretch adopted the name rue de Montmorency in 1768. During the Revolution, between 1793 and 1806, the thoroughfare was named rue de la Réunion, before reverting to its former name in 1808.

The rue de l'Homme Armé formed one section of what is now the rue des Archives, running between the rue Sainte-Croix de la Bretonnerie and the rue des Blancs Manteaux. Other sections of this long thoroughfare had distinct histories. The rue des Deux Portes, at its southern end, was known in the late 13th century as rue Entre Deux Portes and in the 17th century as rue de la Galiace. The adjoining rue des Billettes was called rue des Jardins in the 13th century, and rue Où Dieu fut bouilli or rue du Dieu Bouliz in the 15th century. Further north, the rue du Chaume, rue du Grand Chantier, and rue des Enfants Rouges were opened in the late 13th century, initially forming the rue Neuve-du-Temple.

In 1232, the street was recorded as the rue de Lagny, dite de la Grande Bretonnerie, or simply rue de la Grande Bretonnerie, and was also known as rue Sainte-Croix. The section of the street that opened onto the rue du Temple carried specific names in later centuries: in the 14th century it was called rue Agnès la Buschère or Agnès la Huschère, and by the early 15th century it was recorded under the names rue Dame Agnès l'Asnière and Dame Agnès la Vachère.

Over the centuries, the street name underwent numerous variations, including rue du Bourtibou, du Bourc Tibout, du Bouc Thibout, du Bourg Thiboud, du Beautibourg, and rue du Bourg Thiébault. The present street also includes a portion of the former place du Marché Saint-Jean, situated between the rue de la Verrerie and the rue de Rivoli. That square existed at the end of the 13th century under the name place du cimetière Saint-Jean, later becoming place du Vieux Cimetière Saint-Jean. During the French Revolution, the square bore the name place des Droits de l'Homme.

In the 16th century, the street was also known as the rue du Puits and the rue du Champ Gaillard. A section about 37 metres long, extending beyond the cul-de-sac portion, was decommissioned by order of 20 November 1957 so that it could be incorporated into the École Polytechnique. Later, the cul-de-sac section itself was absorbed into the rue Jacques-Henri Lartigue by municipal decree on 18 July 1995.

The street formerly comprised two distinct sections: the rue Neuve Saint-Laurent, running between the rue du Temple and the rue Volta, and the rue du Vertbois, extending between the rue Volta and the rue Saint-Martin. Historically, it was also referred to as the rue Gaillardbois. The section located between the rue de Turbigo and the rue du Temple was suppressed pursuant to a decree of 11 February 1865 during the opening of the rue de Turbigo.

The older portion of this thoroughfare was known over time as the passage au Maire, rue au Mayre, impasse du Roi de Rome, and rue de Rome. The stretch situated between the rue Volta and the rue des Vertus absorbed the cul-de-sac de Rome. The street was also recorded under several variant names and spellings, including rue Aumair, Aumaire, Homer, and Aumère.

The modern street incorporates several older thoroughfares. The section once known as the rue Beaubourg opened at the end of the 11th century, crossing the city wall; inside the wall it was called the rue de la Poterne and later rue de la Fausse Poterne, while outside it was the rue outre la Poterne Nicolas Hydron. The former rue Transnonain was opened near the start of the 13th century and bore successive names including rue de Châlons, rue Trousse Nonnain, rue Trace put..., and rue Tasse Nonnain. Further north, the former passage au Maire was originally called the passage Bailly, while the rue Saint-Hugues was opened around 1780. In 1972, part of the street was removed to construct the national centre of contemporary art.

Running from the rue Beaubourg to the rue Saint-Martin, the street recorded a sequence of names associated with performers. In the 13th century it was recorded as the vicus Joculatorum, and by 1325 it was known as the rue des Jongleurs or rue aux Jongleurs. At the beginning of the 15th century it was called the rue des Ménestrels, a name that evolved by 1842 into the rue des Ménétriers, shortly before it was absorbed into the rue Rambuteau.

The section opening onto the rue Saint-Merri was known towards the end of the 13th century as the rue Aufroy des Grès (vicus Aufridi de Gressibus) and later as the rue Espaulart. The portion between the rue du Renard and the rue Brisemiche, recorded in the tax roll of 1313, was variously rendered as vicus Petri Oilart, rue Pierre Allard, rue O'Lard, Aulard, or Aulart. A police decree ordered the closure of the street on 5 April 1817. In 1972, part of it was suppressed for the construction of the national centre of contemporary art.

In 1321, the street was recorded under several variants: the rue Saint-Landry, the rue du Port Saint-Landry, and the grande rue Saint-Landry sur l'Yaue. By the 16th century, it was designated as the rue Basse du Port Saint-Landry. At another point in its history, the street was also known by the name rue d'Enfer, or via Inferior.

The southern portion, formerly known as the rue Saint-Nicolas du Chardonnet and even earlier as Saint-Nicolas près du Puits, appears to have been opened around 1246. The name rue des Bernardins is first documented in a confiscations account dating from 1427. The dead-end section extending beyond the rue des Écoles was later opened by the City of Paris.

The thoroughfare originally extended all the way from the rue Copeau—now the rue Lacépède—to the place Maubert. Its outer sections were long known as the rue du Faubourg Saint-Victor. By a decree of 2 October 1865, the section between the place Jussieu and the rue Lacépède was renamed the rue Linné. A few years later, a prefectoral order on 3 September 1869 merged the stretch running between the rue des Fossés Saint-Bernard and the place Jussieu into the rue Jussieu.

The thoroughfare is documented as existing in the 13th century. Between 1266 and 1276, it was known as the rue Sainte-Geneviève, and later as Sainte-Geneviève la Grant, Sainte-Geneviève du Mont, rue du Mont, and rue des Boucheries. During the Revolutionary era, from 1793 until 1815, its name was shortened simply to the rue de la Montagne.

The section between the rue Beaubourg and the rue du Temple was known in 1328 as the ruelle au Villain, later becoming the rue Cour au Villain. The cartographer Lacaille recorded it under the names rue Courtauvillain and ruelle Auvillain. This eastern segment adopted the name rue de Montmorency in 1768. During the Revolution, between 1793 and 1806, the entire street was renamed the rue de la Réunion, before reverting to its earlier name in 1808.

The street is recorded on the tax roll of 1313 under the name Jehan Palée, and was subsequently known as the rue Palée and the rue Saint-Julien. It was later called the rue de la Poterne, the rue de la Fausse Poterne, and the rue Jetty. Other historical designations included the cour du More dite des Anglais and the cour des Anglais ou du More, before it was officially named the rue du Maure.

The modern street was formed by combining two older thoroughfares. Its southern portion was originally the rue des Cinq Diamants, so called from 1536, having previously carried the names rue de la Couréerie, rue de la Courroirie, and rue de la Vieille Courroierie. Over time, the name Quincampoix was rendered as Cinquampoit, Quiquenpoit by Jacques Androuet du Cerceau, and Quinquempoix by Jean-Baptiste-Michel Jaillot. The street was also known as the rue de la Confréerie.

The long street absorbed several distinct historical sections. At its southern end, the rue Planche Mibray ran between the quai de Gesvres and the avenue Victoria. North of this, the section known as the rue des Arcis was recorded as Vicus de Arsionibus in 1195, rue des Assis in 1218, and rue des Arsis or rue des Ars in 1254. Further north, the stretch between the rue de la Verrerie and the rue Saint-Merri was variously called the rue Saint-Merri, rue de l'Archet Saint-Merri, and rue de la Porte Saint-Merri, while the section reaching to the boulevard Saint-Martin was named the rue Saint-Martin des Champs.

Before its removal, the street began at the rue de la Coutellerie and ended at the rue des Arcis, now the rue Saint-Martin. By a prefectoral decree of 11 March 1851, it was briefly designated as part of the former rue des Écrivains. Earlier historians recorded alternative names for the passage: Henri Sauval claimed it had been known as the rue du Croc, whereas the 16th-century map of the Tapisserie assigned it the name of la Radrerie.

The surviving section of the street between the avenue Victoria and the rue de Rivoli occupies the site of the old rue de la Tacherie, which originally stretched between the rue de la Coutellerie and the former rue Jean Pain Mollet. Over the centuries, the street was recorded under several variants of its name, including the rue de la Juiverie Saint-Bon in 1261, the rue de la Vieille Juiverie in 1273, and the rue de l'Attacherie or de la Tacherie by 1300.

The list of former names recorded for the street is extensive. It was known in various periods as the rue des Recommanderesses or de la Commanderesse, the rue de la Vieille Oreille (also spelled Guignoreille or Guigne Oreille), the rue Guillori, and the rue de la Coifferie or aux Coiffeurs, alongside rue de la Coutellerie or des Couteliers. These historical designations applied specifically to the stretch of the street running between the former rue du Mouton and the former rue Jean de l'Épine.

The street originally ran from the place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville to the rue Saint-Martin. In the 14th century, this thoroughfare and the adjoining rue Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie were combined under the single designation of Vannerie. By the 16th century, the section closest to the rue Saint-Martin was known separately as the rue des Recommanderesses. The entire street was eliminated in the 19th century when the avenue Victoria was cut through.

Running from the place de l'Hôtel-de-Ville to the rue Saint-Martin, the street took its name from the tanners who worked there. In earlier times it was known as the rue de l'Écorcherie, referring to the flaying of animal hides. According to the 17th-century historian Henri Sauval, the passage was also known at one time as the ruelle de la Planche aux Teinturiers. It was completely cleared when the avenue Victoria was laid out across the district.

The street underwent several changes of name before its final destruction. In the work of Guillot around 1300 it was named rue Glateingni, and it also acquired the popular name rue du Val d'Amour. By 1380 it was documented as the rue du Chevet Saint-Denis de la Chartre, referring to the apsidal end of the neighbouring church of Saint-Denis-de-la-Chartre. In its final period it was called the rue du Haut Moulin, before being suppressed by a decree of 22 May 1865 for the construction of the new Hôtel-Dieu hospital.

The street stretched from the place du Parvis to the former rue du Marché-Palu. Constructed in 1163 under the simple name of rue Neuve, it became known as Neuve Notre-Dame towards the end of the 13th century. During the French Revolution, it was temporarily renamed the rue de la Raison. The thoroughfare eventually ceased to exist as an independent street when it was incorporated into the expanded expanse of the place du Parvis Notre-Dame.

Originally running from the rue de la Bûcherie to the rue Galande, this Left Bank street was known historically under several names, including rue Pavée, rue du Pavé de la place Maubert, and rue d'Amboise. Between 1806 and 1912, the passage was formally merged into the space of the place Maubert itself, before being separated again and subsequently given its modern designation.

The street is documented from the beginning of the 13th century. By 1247, it was recorded under several related names: the rue des Plâtriers, de la Plâtrière, or de la Plâtrerie, as well as the rue Rodolphe le Plâtrier. By the 15th century, it had come to be known simply as the rue du Plâtre, and was later designated as the rue du Plâtre Saint-Jacques prior to its modern renaming.

The creation of the boulevard Saint-Germain led to the absorption or destruction of dozens of ancient Left Bank streets and alleys. A section of the rue des Noyers was initially taken over by the main thoroughfare, and the remaining portion of the street was officially incorporated into the boulevard by a prefectoral decree issued on 26 December 1893.

Laid out at the start of the 14th century through the Clos Bruneau vineyard, the street was initially called the rue du Clos Bruneau or rue du Clos Brunel. By 1370, records refer to it as the rue du Clos Bruneau dite Jean de Beauvais. It subsequently took the name rue Saint-Jean de Beauvais before acquiring its modern form.

The street originally ran from the rue de la Montagne Sainte-Geneviève to the rue des Carmes. In 1243, it was known as the rue Judas. Large portions of the street were eliminated during the construction of the boulevard Saint-Germain, leaving only a surviving stub, which retains the name of Clos Bruneau.

Over the centuries, different segments of this major Left Bank arterial road bore a succession of names, including grand'rue Saint-Jacques des Prêcheurs, grand'rue Saint-Étienne des Grès, grand'rue Saint-Benoît Le Bestournet, grand'rue près du chevet de l'Église Saint-Séverin, grand'rue oultre Petit Pont, grand'rue vers Saint-Matelin, and grand'rue Saint-Benoît. Officially named rue Saint-Jacques in 1806, its layout was altered in 1974 when a portion was incorporated into the place Alphonse-Laveran in front of the Val-de-Grâce military hospital.

Running from the former rue de Reims to the rue Saint-Étienne-des-Grès (now the rue Cujas), this street originally bore the name rue Saint-Symphorien des Vignes or Saint-Symphorien. It is also recorded as having been named Jean le Maître, while Jean Boisseau referred to it as the rue des Vignes. In the 17th century it was known as the petite rue Sainte-Barbe before taking its final name from the Collège des Cholets built along it. It was abolished by royal ordinance on 5 September 1845.

The modern street was formed by merging three older thoroughfares under an order of 2 April 1868. The section between the rue Saint-Martin and the rue Saint-Denis was the original rue Greneta, recorded in earlier forms as rue d'Arnetal, Darnetal, Dernetat, Drenetat, Darnestat, or rue de la Trinité. The section between the rue Saint-Denis and the rue Dussoubs existed in 1313 as the rue Percée (or Perciée) and by 1383 as the rue du Renard. The section between the rue Dussoubs and the rue Montorgueil existed in 1255, successively named Bellus Locus, Bellus Reditus (1258), and Beaurepaire (1313).

In the 13th century, parts of this road were known as the Sellerie de Paris and the Sellerie de la Grande Rue, as well as the grand'rue de Paris. By the 14th century, it was recorded under titles including the grande rue or rue des Saints Innocents, and the grant chaussée de Monsieur or grant chaussée de Monseigneur Saint-Denis. During the French Revolution, the street was temporarily renamed the rue de Franciade.

The street ran between the former rue du Bourg-l'Abbé and the rue Saint-Denis. From 1242 until 1540, it was documented as the rue Jean Palée or rue Palée. On the 17th-century plan of Blondel, it appears under the name rue du Petit Leu. The passage was destroyed in the 1850s to make way for the boulevard de Sébastopol.

The modern street combines several older sections. The stretch between the rue Saint-Denis and the rue Dussoubs was recorded as the rue du Lion d'Or in 1360, rue du Lion in 1421, and rue du Grand Lion in 1474, as well as rue Pavée Saint-Sauveur, rue de l'Arbalète or des Arbalétriers (according to Sauval), and rue Paule on Ducerceau's plan. The section between the rue Dussoubs and the rue Montorgueil was known as the rue Pavée from 1313 until its merger with the rue du Petit Lion in 1851. The original rue Tiquetonne, running between the rue Montorgueil and the rue Montmartre, had previously been called rue Denis le Coffrier in 1372 and rue Quiquetonne in 1400.

In the 13th century, the street stretched all the way between the rue Saint-Martin and the rue Saint-Denis. Its name evolved from earlier spellings such as rue As Oues, aux Oues, or aux Oës. In 1881, the section of the street lying between the boulevard de Sébastopol and the rue Saint-Denis was detached to form part of the rue Étienne-Marcel.

The present street brings together two older sections. While the western part between the rue Quincampoix and the rue Saint-Denis was the rue Troussevache (in existence by 1248), the eastern part between the rue Saint-Martin and the rue Quincampoix was formerly the rue Ogniard. Mentioned in a document of 1260, that eastern section was known in the 13th century as the rue Almari or Almarici de Roissiaco, and later as rue Amauri or Emauri de Roissy, Oignart (1493), Hoignart (1495), Hungard, Hougnart, Oniard, Aniac, Haumard, or rue Marie de Poissy.

Built up by 1250, the rue des Lombards originally ran between the rue Saint-Martin and the rue Saint-Denis, and was known in the 14th century as the rue de la Buffeterie or des Lombards. A portion of it is recorded as the rue de la Pourpointerie in 1612 and 1636. By a decree of 1 February 1877, it absorbed the rue de l'Aiguillerie (between the rue Saint-Denis and the rue Sainte-Opportune), which Henri Sauval called the rue de l'Esquillerie and which had reportedly borne the name rue Alain de Dampierre in 1220.

Running between the former rue de la Vieille-Monnaie and the rue Saint-Denis, the street was recorded in 1300 as the rue de la Hiaumerie or Hyaumerie, deriving from the helmets crafted there, and was also known as the rue des Armuriers. By a prefectoral order on 11 March 1851, it was briefly renamed as part of the rue des Écrivains before being entirely removed during the clearing of the rue de Rivoli.

The street connected the former rue Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie with the former rue de la Heaumerie. It had borne the name of the soap-makers since the beginning of the 14th century. The thoroughfare was wiped out in the 1850s when the rue de Rivoli was driven through the neighbourhood.

The street ran from the rue Saint-Denis to the former rue de la Vieille-Harengerie. According to the 16th-century plan of Jacques Androuet du Cerceau, both this street and the adjoining rue du Chevalier-du-Guet were designated by the name rue de la Serpente. It was cleared away during the creation of the rue de Rivoli.

Documented since the beginning of the 13th century, the street originally extended all the way south to the quai de la Mégisserie on the bank of the Seine. By a municipal decree on 16 July 1912, its southernmost section, lying between the quai de la Mégisserie and the avenue Victoria, was detached and renamed the rue Édouard-Colonne.

The street ran between the rue de la Cité and the rue de la Barillerie. According to older documents, it was originally called the rue Macra Madiana. The cartographer Lacaille later recorded it as the rue de la Vieille Pelleterie, though the furriers' name had been used since 1183. Around 1806 it was renamed the rue Desaix, before reverting to the rue de la Pelleterie in 1814.

Before its redevelopment, the street ran from the rue de la Juiverie to the place du Palais de Justice. Known as the rue de la Draperie in 1293, it became the rue de la Vieille Draperie by 1313. Today its former course is covered by the rue de Lutèce and a portion of the place Louis Lépine.

In the 13th century, this thoroughfare was known as the street leading from the Petit-Pont to the place Saint-Michel—referring to the square in front of the palace chapel—or simply the rue Saint-Michel. It was also recorded as the rue du Marché Palu and the rue de la Grant Orberie, or de l'Herberie. By 1280 it had acquired the name Calande, derived either from a house owned by Jean de la Kalendre in 1343 or from a property belonging to Nicolas le Kalendreur.

Before being renamed impasse Hautefeuille, the surviving cul-de-sac was known as impasse Percée. In the 14th century, after its 1262 appearance as the rue Percée, the street was recorded as the rue Percée dite des Deux Portes, the rue des Deux Portes, and subsequently the rue Percée Saint-André.

The original 13th-century name stems from Erembourg (or Eremburge) de Brie, recorded in Latin as Eremburgis de Bria. Over time, popular corruption produced various transitional spellings including Bourg de Brie, Bourc de Brie, Boudebrie, Bout de Brye, and Bouttebrie, before settling into its modern form.

The street appears under the Latin name Vicus Tortuosus in a deed of 1263. By the late 13th century it was known as the rue de la Serpent or rue de la Serpente, and several 16th-century maps label it rue Serpente.

The eastern section absorbed in 1851, previously the rue du Battoir-Saint-André between the rue Hautefeuille and the rue de l'Éperon, had its own long history. It was recorded in 1292 as the rue Jehan de Fontenoy (or Jean de Fontenay) and called the rue de la Plâtrière by Guillot in 1300. Later records refer to it as the Haulte Rue or rue du Bastouer, as well as the rue de la Vieille Plâtrière, before it took the name rue Serpente in 1521.

Towards the end of the 13th century, the street was known as the rue o Fain. In 1383 it was recorded as the rue aux Moines de Cernay, before reverting to its earlier name in the 15th century. It was also referred to at times as the rue Servode. Briefly designated as part of the rue des Noyers by a prefectural decree on 10 May 1851, the thoroughfare was destroyed shortly afterwards by the creation of the boulevard Saint-Germain.

Different sections of the street bore distinct names over the centuries. The stretch between the rue de l'École de Médecine and the rue Monsieur le Prince was known as the rue Saint-Côme et rue Saint-Damien from 1254 to 1279, and later as the rue aux Hoirs d'Harcourt. The section between the rue Saint-Séverin and the rue de l'École de Médecine appeared in Latin records as vicus Cithare in Judearia (1247) and vicus Harpe (1270).

The northernmost section, formerly the rue de la Vieille Boucherie between the rue de la Huchette and the rue Saint-Séverin, held names such as vicus Reginaldi dicti le Harpeur (1265) and rue de l'Abreuvoir Mâcon (1391).

In 1792 during the Revolution, the street received the name rue Catinat, but returned to rue de la Sorbonne in 1802. In 1934, the section between the rue des Écoles and the rue Du Sommerard was absorbed into the place Paul Painlevé.

The street originally ran from the rue Saint-Jacques to the rue Neuve des Poirées. It was recorded as the rue Thomas d'Argenteuil in 1236 and the rue Guillaume d'Argenteuil in 1254. In 1443 it was popularly known as the rue aux Écoliers de Rethel after the college established there. Later identified as the rue Grenouiller or Grenouillière on Abbé Delagrive's map, it was extended to the place de la Sorbonne in 1824 and renamed rue Gerson by imperial decree in 1864 before being eliminated.

Originally known as the rue Neuve de l'Ursine before taking the name rue des Filles Dieu, the street existed by 1530 near the convent. In 1643, a portion of it was called the rue Saint-Guillaume. Later in 1884, when the section running between the rue Saint-Denis and the rue Saint-Spire was realigned, it led to the destruction of the impasse de la Grosse Tête.

By an order of 2 April 1868, the rue du Renard Saint-Sauveur was combined with the rue Beaurepaire and the rue Greneta into a single street. The middle section, formerly the rue Beaurepaire between the rue Dussoubs and the rue Montorgueil, was recorded in 1255 as Bellus Locus, in 1258 as Bellus Reditus, and in 1313 as Beaurepaire. Meanwhile, the eastern section (rue Greneta) between the rue Saint-Martin and the rue Saint-Denis had older forms such as rue d'Arnetal, Darnetal, or Darnestat, and was also known as the rue de la Trinité.

The section between the rue Montmartre and the rue Mauconseil originally bore several names, including rue Nicolas Arrode, rue au Comte d'Artois, and rue de la Porte au Comte (or à la Comtesse) d'Artois. First joined to the rue Montorgueil in 1792, this section reverted to the name rue de la Comtesse d'Artois in 1814, before being permanently merged into the rue Montorgueil in 1830.

The modern rue Tiquetonne was formed by merging several earlier streets. The section between the rue Saint-Denis and the rue Dussoubs was known as the rue du Lion d'Or in 1360, the rue du Lion in 1421, and the rue du Grand Lion in 1474, as well as the rue Pavée Saint-Sauveur and the rue Paule on Ducerceau's map.

The section between the rue Dussoubs and the rue Montorgueil kept the name rue Pavée from 1313 until 1851. Farther west, between the rue Montorgueil and the rue Montmartre, the old rue Tiquetonne had been called the rue Denis le Coffrier in 1372 and the rue Quiquetonne in 1400.

The section running between the rue de Turbigo and the rue Étienne-Marcel went through several successive names after its initial creation, being called the rue Neuve de Bourgogne and the rue Neuve Saint-François before becoming the rue Françoise and eventually the rue Française.

Running between the rue Montmartre and the rue Mauconseil, the street held several early names, including rue Nicolas Arrode and rue de la Porte au Comte (or à la Comtesse) d'Artois. Following its first merger into the rue Montorgueil in 1792, it briefly returned to the name rue de la Comtesse d'Artois in 1814, before being permanently reincorporated into the rue Montorgueil in 1830.

The Revolutionary renaming to rue Bonconseil lasted from 1792 to 1806, and the street was also written as rue Monconseil. Originally extending as far as the rue Saint-Denis, the eastern stretch between the rue Mondétour and the rue Saint-Denis appears under the name rue Saint-Jacques de l'Hôpital on Mérian's map.

Previously known as the ruelle Jean Gilles, the lane ran from the rue de la Grande Truanderie to the rue du Cygne. In the 11th century it was recorded as Montdétor and Maldestor. Its spelling shifted through Maudestour or Maudétour in the 14th century, Maudestour in the 15th century, and Maudétour in the 18th century, before taking its modern spelling Mondétour in the 19th century.

Before taking its modern name, the thoroughfare was designated as the rue du Four Saint-Honoré or simply the rue du Four. In 1936, during the expansion of the Halles Centrales, the northern section running between the rue Berger and the junction of the rue Coquillière and the rue Rambuteau was incorporated directly into the central market complex.

The northern section between the rue Berger and the rue Rambuteau was absorbed into the Halles complex. Over the centuries, the street's name appeared in various written forms, including the rue des Prévoires, Provoires, Preuvoires, Prouvoires, Provaires, and rue Prouvelle.

In earlier times, the thoroughfare had been known as the rue de la Ganterie. The section located between the rue des Innocents and the rue Berger was formally decommissioned by a decree of 30 August 1972 as part of the Forum Central des Halles redevelopment project, leading to its suppression.

The street brought together several historic sections. The section known as the rue de l'Arche Marion existed in 1300. At the start of the 14th century, it was called the rue de l'Abreuvoir Thibaut aux Dés, later the rue des Jardins, and then the ruelle Jean de la Poterne. In 1530 it became the rue des Étuves or des Étuves aux Femmes, before taking the name rue de l'Abreuvoir Marion or de l'Arche Marion. The middle section, the rue Thibault aux Dés, existed in 1230 under the Latin name Théobaldi ad Decios. By the end of the 13th century, the section called the rue des Bourdonnais was named after Adam Bourdon and Guillaume Bourdon, before settling into its modern name at the beginning of the 14th century.

The street ran from the rue des Bourdonnais to the rue de la Monnaie before its demolition for the construction of the rue de Rivoli. In earlier times, it included the section of the rue des Fossés Saint-Germain l'Auxerrois extending as far as the rue de l'Arbre Sec. In the 13th century, the stretch running from the rue Tirechappe to the rue des Bourdonnais carried the name rue de la Charpenterie.

In 1300 the street carried the name rue Saint-Germain à Couroiers, before being known as the rue Saint-Germain or grande rue Saint-Germain. A section between the rue des Bourdonnais and the rue de la Monnaie, measuring about 40 metres beyond numbers 23 and 36, was removed by decree on 24 February 1882.

Known since the 13th century under names such as Gilles le Queux or Guy le Queux in 1275, the street was called Gui le Preux and Gui le Comte in the 14th century. By 1540 it was written as Gilles Queux, Guille Queulx, Villequeux, Lequeux, and Gist le Cœur, alongside Gilles le Cœur in Corrozet. It was also referred to as the rue des Deux Moutons, and in 1639 as the rue du Battoir. It is also said to have been called rue du Rasoir.

The street appeared under various medieval spellings, recorded as rue Hyrondale in 1224, rue Hyrundal in 1257, de Lyrundelle in 1262, and rue Hérondale in 1300. Before part of it was removed to build the place Saint-Michel, the street formerly extended all the way from the rue Gît-le-Cœur to the former place du Pont Saint-Michel.

The street originally extended as far as the rue Serpente. Early forms of its name include Guidonis ad Pictavinas in 1288, Grimaud ad Pictavinas in 1291, Guiart as Poitevins in 1292, Ginart aux Poitevins in 1300, Gérard aux Poitevins in 1358, grant rue des Poitevins, and rue Poitevine in 1448. The section turning back onto the rue Serpente, which was removed when the rue Danton was opened under a decree of 6 April 1895, had carried the names rue du Pet in 1396, rue du Petit Pet in 1560, and rue du Gros Pet in Gilles Corrozet's 1532 guide.

The section of the street between the rue Saint-André des Arts and the rue des Poitevins originally had several distinct names. It was initially called the rue de la Barre, before being known as the rue du Chevet Saint-André, the rue Saint-André, and also the rue de la Vieille Plâtrière.

The street is mentioned under the name Vicus Tortuosus in an act from 1263, and by the end of the 13th century it was known as the rue de la Serpent or rue de la Serpente. The section between the rue Hautefeuille and the rue de l'Éperon, formerly the rue du Battoir Saint-André, was called rue Jehan de Fontenoy or Jean de Fontenay in 1292. The poet Guillot recorded it as rue de la Plâtrière in 1300. Later sources referred to it as Haulte Rue or rue du Bastouer, as well as rue de la Vieille Plâtrière, before it was named rue Serpente in 1521.

In 1304 the street was designated under the names Saint-Côme and Saint-Damien. Prior to 1672 it was called the rue Saint-Germain, and from 1672 to 1690 the rue des Cordeliers. During the French Revolution, after taking the name rue de l'École de Médecine in 1790, it was renamed rue Marat in 1793 and rue de l'École de Santé in Year IV of the revolutionary calendar, before reverting to rue de l'École de Médecine shortly after. A section between the rue Dupuytren and the rue du Four was later absorbed into the boulevard Saint-Germain.

The street brought together several historical sections. The section between the rue Saint-Denis and the rue Dussoubs was called rue du Lion d'Or in 1360, rue du Lion in 1421, and rue du Grand Lion in 1474. It was also known as rue Pavée Saint-Sauveur, rue du Petit Lion, rue de l'Arbalète or des Arbalétriers according to Henri Sauval, and rue Paule on Jacques Androuet du Cerceau's map. The section between the rue Dussoubs and the rue Montorgueil was named rue Pavée in 1313. Before the creation of the rue Étienne Marcel, the original rue Tiquetonne ran between the rue Montorgueil and the rue Montmartre; it was recorded as rue Denis le Coffrier in 1372 and rue Quiquetonne in 1400.

In the 14th century, the section of the street running between the church of Saint-Eustache and the rue d'Aboukir was known as the rue de la Porte Montmartre. During the French Revolution, the street was given the name rue Montmarat.

The street was made up of two historical sections. The section formerly extending as far as the rue Coquillière bore names including rue de Guernelles, Guarnelle, Guarnales, Garnelles, and Grenelle Saint-Honoré, while Jacques Androuet du Cerceau recorded it as Cernelles. The other section was originally called rue Maverse before becoming the rue Plâtrière. The street as a whole was also known as the rue de la Poste.

Before taking the name rue des Vieilles Étuves Saint-Honoré, the street was known as rue des Étuves or rue des Estuves, and earlier still as the rue du Pressoir du Bret. The section between the rue Berger and the rue de Viarmes was named rue Marie de France by municipal decision in April 2025.

The street originally ran between the rue Saint-Honoré and the rue des Deux Écus, and formerly extended as far as the place Saint-Eustache. In early times it carried the name Nesle, and later Behaigne or Vieille Behaigne, references to Bohemia in 1328. It adopted the name Orléans around 1388. During the 16th century it was also designated as the street of the Filles Repenties and Filles Pénitentes. Following its partial removal for the construction of the rue du Louvre in 1888, what remained of the street was incorporated into the rue du Louvre by prefectoral order on 18 April 1890.

The street appeared under various historical names, including Oteriche, Osteriche, Hoteriche, Hosteriche, Autheriche, and d'Autruche or d'Autruche dite du Louvre. It was called rue du Louvre in 1600. Although much of the street was removed when the Louvre was enlarged in 1664, the surviving portion became the rue de l'Oratoire, which was still recorded as the rue de l'Autruche as late as 1732.

The creation of the rue du Louvre led to the suppression of the rue des Poulies between the rue de Rivoli and the rue Saint-Honoré, as well as the rue d'Orléans between the rue Saint-Honoré and the place des Deux Écus. In 1972, the section located between the quai du Louvre and the rue de Rivoli was renamed the rue de l'Amiral de Coligny.

Recorded in 1269 as the rue de l'Abbé de Saint-Denis, the street was subsequently named after the local ecclesiastical foundation as the rue du Collège Saint-Denis, rue des Écoles Saint-Denis, rue des Écoliers de Saint-Denis, and rue des Charités Saint-Denis. The section near the rue Saint-André des Arts is said to have carried the names rue de la Barre, rue des Barres, and rue de l'Hôtel de Nemours in earlier times.

The street bore a sequence of names across its history, including rue de Laas, rue Saint-Germain or rue Saint-Germain des Prés in 1332, rue Saint-André, rue Saint-Andrieu, rue Saint-André de Laas, and finally rue Saint-André des Arcs. In the course of its development, it also absorbed the former rue de la Clef.

The street ran from the old rue du Jardinet to the rue de l'École de Médecine. It took the name rue Larrey by presidential decree on 9 April 1851, which was the name it bore at the time it was suppressed during the construction of the boulevard Saint-Germain.

The street was recorded under several variants of its main name, including rue Sainte-Marie l'Égyptienne, rue de l'Égyptienne, rue de l'Égyptienne de Blois, rue de la Gipecienne in the 15th century, and rue de la Gyptienne, de l'Egizziane, or de l'Ajussiane. In the 16th century it was also known as rue du Coq Héron and rue du Coq Héron, dite l'Égyptienne.

In the mid-16th century, several houses bordering the street near the quay were demolished to create the place des Trois Maries. This square lay between the quai du Louvre and the rue des Prêtres Saint-Germain l'Auxerrois until it was suppressed by decree on 24 February 1882. The street itself was widened following decrees of the King's Council of State issued on 31 January 1689 and 24 February 1693.

One section previously extended as far as the rue Coquillière, bearing variants such as rue de Guernelles, Guarnelle, Guarnales, Garnelles, de Guernelle Saint-Honoré and Grenelle Saint-Honoré. Another section was originally called rue Maverse, then rue Plâtrière. The street was also known as the rue de la Poste.

Between the rue de l'Arbre Sec and the now deleted rue du Rempart, it was known in the 13th and 14th centuries as the rue de la Croix du Trahoir or Croix du Tiroir, and by 1450 as the rue de la Chaussée Saint-Honoré. Further west, between the rue du Rempart and the rue Royale, its older names included the chemin de Clichy (1204), grand chemin Saint-Honoré (1283), chemin Royal (1393), nouvelle rue Saint-Louis (1407), and rue Neuve Saint-Honoré (1638). In 1966, the stretch between the Palais Royal, the Théâtre Français and place André Malraux became the place Colette.

The street ran from the rue du Champ Fleuri to the rue Froidmanteau. In the 13th century it was recorded as Biauvoir or Byauvoir, changing to Beauvoir in 1372 and Beauvais in 1450 before its removal between 1806 and 1808.

Historical records cite several other names for the street: rue du Puys in 1360, chemin de Cassel or rue Cassel dite du Colombier between 1411 and 1453, rue de la Maladerie in 1414, and rue du Puys Mauconseil from 1506 to 1514. Between 1509 and 1524 it appeared as grant rue Saint-Sulpice and rue des Champs, and in 1521 as rue Saint-Sulpice. On the 1615 Mérian map it is named rue de la Pelleterie.

Earlier documents record various names for the route: rue de Vaulgirard (1523), chemin des Carrières de Vaugirard (1529), chemin de Bel Ayr (1547), rue de Bel Air (1559), and rue des Vaches (1543 and 1627). Between the rue de Condé and rue Cassette, documents from the 14th to 16th centuries refer to it as the chemin or voie des Ruelles, and in 1355 as the voie du Valgirard. In 1965, the intersection of the rues Rotrou, Corneille, and de Médicis along its course was named place Paul Claudel.

The street was widened near the place des Victoires under a decree of the Conseil du Roi on 22 June 1685. The section between the rue Coquillière and the place des Victoires was once called the rue d'Aubusson, while the rue La Vrillière formerly formed part of the street.

At the time it was suppressed, the street ran from the rue du Carrousel to the place du Palais Royal, having previously begun at the rue des Orties du Louvre before 1808. During the French Revolution, it was known as the rue Thomas du Muséum.

The street was referred to under several descriptive names, including chemin du Pré aux Clercs, chemin du Pilori au Pré aux Clercs, and from 1489, rue de Seine. According to the historian Sauval, it also bore the name rue Dauphine. A prefectural decree of 26 February 1867 temporarily named it rue du Sénat.

In 1296 the road was recorded as the rue de la Granche Jehan le Bouvier. During the 14th century it was known as the grant rue Saint-Germain and chaussée du Roi (1398), and in the 15th century as the grant rue du Four, rue du Bourg (1412), rue de la Maladerye (1413), and chemin de Vaugirard (1428). The section between the rue Montfaucon and rue des Cannettes was called rue de la Blanche Oie before becoming rue du Four Saint-Germain.

The street ran from the rue Saint-Martin to the now vanished rue du Bourg l'Abbé. Documented in 1253 under the variants Heuleu, Huleu, and Hue Leu, it was also known at times as the rue du Pet and the rue des Innocents.

The university hospital is located at 78 rue du Général-Leclerc in the commune of Le Kremlin-Bicêtre, in Val-de-Marne. It forms part of the Assistance publique – Hôpitaux de Paris (AP-HP), occupying the site of the former hospice founded in the 17th century.

Mentioned since the Early Middle Ages, Reuilly hosted a royal castle from the Merovingian era until the reign of Jean le Bon in the 14th century. During the Middle Ages the Templars received a land donation here. A village emerged in the 17th century and was attached to Paris in 1702.

The name originally designated a garden attached to a farm. La Courtille served as the starting point for the annual carnival parade known as the descente de la Courtille. Although absent from modern Paris street names, a large housing complex built in 1980 near Ménilmontant metro station—stretching from the rue Oberkampf to the boulevard de Belleville in the 11th arrondissement—is named Les Courtilles in memory of the hamlet.

When the former commune was annexed in 1860, a small portion was assigned to Saint-Ouen, while the rest formed the 18th arrondissement alongside the quarters of Grandes-Carrières, Clignancourt, La Goutte-d'Or, and La Chapelle. Traditionally bounded by the rue Custine, rue Caulaincourt, boulevards de Clichy and Rochechouart, and rue de Clignancourt, the hill contains the highest natural elevation in Paris at 130.53 metres.

At the time of its removal during the expansion of the Louvre, the street ran from the rue du Carrousel to the place du Palais-Royal. Prior to 1808, its course had originated at the rue des Orties du Louvre. First documented as the rue des Chanoines in 1212, it took the name rue Saint-Thomas du Louvre in 1242, and was later designated as the rue Thomas du Muséum during the French Revolution.

One of the historic suburbs of Paris, the faubourg Saint-Honoré developed around its central thoroughfare, the rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré. This street itself forms an extension of the rue Saint-Honoré. Historically, it served as the extra-muros continuation of the rue Saint-Honoré beyond the city walls known as the enceinte des Fossés jaunes.

In the 16th century, Chaillot developed following the construction of a château for Queen Catherine de Médicis, alongside other large residences and religious institutions such as the couvent de Chaillot. The original parish territory was twice as large as the modern administrative quarter, extending along the Seine from the Passy cemetery to the modern place de la Concorde. In 1659, Chaillot officially became a suburb of the capital and was divided in 1785 by the Wall of the Farmers-General. For the 1878 Universal Exposition, the Palais du Trocadéro was built on the hill, around which many residential buildings were later erected.

The former law court and prison stands on the western part of the Île de la Cité, beneath the Palais de Justice. It originally formed part of the old royal residence, the Palais de la Cité, which also included the Sainte-Chapelle. After being tried and condemned here during the French Revolution, prisoners were sent on to various locations around Paris to be executed by guillotine. The site is now preserved as a national monument under the administration of the Centre des monuments nationaux.

This residence between court and garden, set in the heart of the Latin Quarter, takes its name from the abbots of Cluny who taught at the nearby Collège de Cluny and made it their home from the 13th century. Between the 17th century and the French Revolution, the building accommodated papal nuncios as well as private residents. Rebuilt in the Flamboyant Gothic style with elements of the Louis XII style, its design illustrates the reluctance of Parisian architects to adopt Italian innovations, much like the Tour Saint-Jacques. The state acquired the property in 1843 to establish the museum.

The church is dedicated to Saint Eustace, originally named Placidus or Placidas, a Roman general and hunting enthusiast who converted to Christianity. His symbols and attributes can be seen on both the interior and the exterior of the building. Intertwined letters S and E, hunting horns, and a stag bearing a cross between its antlers appear on pedestals inside the church as well as on the gables of the two transepts outside.
