The school stood in the rue Valette. Following its closure in June 1999, its buildings were remodelled by Louis-Ernest Lheureux (1827–1898) and later rehabilitated by Antoine Stinco. In addition to housing the interuniversity Bibliothèque Sainte-Barbe, the premises now accommodate one of the university centres of Panthéon-Assas University.

Designed by the architect François Blondel, the triumphal arch was built in 1673 to celebrate Louis XIV. It stands in today’s 10th arrondissement on the site of the former Paris gate in the ancient wall of Charles V, whose adjacent walls have since been destroyed. Regarded as one of the most representative monuments of the official art of its era.

Initially built as wooden gallows, probably in 1027 by the high justice of the county of Paris, Montfaucon was transformed shortly after 1303 into a monument. Here the remains of executed prisoners, sometimes decapitated or dismembered, were exposed to the wind and crows, whether they had been executed on site or elsewhere in France. In 1416, during the Hundred Years' War following the Paris uprising, it was remodelled into a spectacular structure with sixteen pillars. This grand gallows went into decline with the accession of Henri IV in 1594 and the end of the Wars of Religion. Its ruins were finally cleared away by the French Revolution, though it retained a powerful place in the French imagination alongside the Bastille and the guillotine.

A Christian cemetery and chapel existed on this site from the sixth or seventh century. By the ninth century, after the Norman invasions, a chapel dedicated to Saint Médard stood along the Roman road from Lutetia to Lyon where it crossed the river Bièvre. A papal bull of Alexander III attested in 1163 that the church and parish belonged to the domain of the abbey of Sainte-Geneviève.

Work on the present building was interrupted in December 1561 during the Wars of Religion by the Tumult of Saint-Médard, a clash between Catholics and Protestants that led to the church being sacked. In 1655, jurisdiction over the parish passed from the abbot of Sainte-Geneviève directly to the archbishop of Paris.

The surrounding area was known in 1126 as the Clos du Chardonnet, named after the wild thistles that grew there before vineyards were planted. In 1230, Pierre, abbot of Saint-Victor, granted land to Guillaume d'Auvergne, bishop of Paris, for a chapel dedicated to Saint Nicholas following the rescue of three sailors shipwrecked on the Seine.

That chapel was replaced by a church in 1243, and then by a larger structure consecrated on 13 May 1425 by Jean de Nanton, bishop of Paris. The church was enlarged in 1545 and received a new bell tower in 1625. It originally faced east onto the rue des Bernardins, separated from the rue Saint-Victor by a diversion canal of the Bièvre.

The wood is a remnant of the forest that covered the surroundings of Paris in antiquity. A charter of 848 records an exchange confirmed by Charles the Bald, and documents after 980 list the woods as royal property. Hugh Capet used it as a hunting ground when residing on the Île de la Cité.

In 1183, Philip Augustus enclosed the forest within a twelve-kilometre wall that stood for six centuries. The park was expanded through acquisitions of arable land and vineyards in 1274 and in 1375 eastward to the Marne. According to legend, Saint Louis rendered justice under an oak tree in these woods.

The name Montreuil derives from the Latin Monasteriolum, meaning small monastery. By 1070, the lordship was held by Morard de Montreuil, a vassal of the king. The village grew in importance alongside the royal presence at nearby Vincennes, centred around the church of Saint-Pierre-Saint-Paul, where King Charles V and his wife Jeanne de Bourbon were baptised.

From 1260, Montreuil supplied water to the castle of Vincennes. In 1360, after suffering in the wars under King John the Good, the villagers were granted exemptions from taxes and forced labour on the condition that they maintained at their own expense the fountains that fed the castle fishpond. These privileges were confirmed in 1363 and 1380.

The name Bercy appeared in the twelfth century, derived from an Old French word meaning sheepfold. At the end of the fifteenth century, the domain was purchased by Antoine Robert, a royal secretary, before passing to the Malon family.

On the 1550 map and other contemporary views, Bercy is shown as a feudal fortress with a donjon, enclosed by stone walls and a fortified gate near the Seine. Downstream stood the manor of La Grange aux Merciers, a lavish residence with three main buildings capable of lodging forty horsemen, along with a windmill and outbuildings. Charles de Malon united the two seigneuries in 1624, later demolishing the fortified manor in 1658 to construct a new chateau.

The oldest settlement here was Savies, an estate granted in 862 by Charles the Bald to the abbey of Saint-Denis. In 1060, King Henry I gave Saint-Martin-des-Champs a large domain that included the farm of Savies. Nearby, the hamlet of Poitronville emerged in the twelfth century; its name was replaced by Belleville from the fifteenth century, first appearing in records in 1451.

Devastated during the Hundred Years' War in 1436, the village grew under Francis I along the road to Romainville. In 1543, a chapel dedicated to Saint John the Baptist and Saint Blaise was built to save residents the long journey to Saint-Merry in Paris.

The hamlet's name comes from Clenini Curtis, named after a Gallo-Roman villa owner. Documented from the thirteenth century on the northern slope of Montmartre, Clignancourt produced grain, cherries, and wine. The fief belonged to the abbey of Saint-Denis in the fourteenth century before passing to wealthy Parisian families.

During the siege of Paris in 1465, troops under Charles, Count of Charolais, ravaged the area. On 9 September, Breton and Burgundian soldiers stripped the vineyards of Clignancourt, harvesting unripe grapes to make wine. In 1569, the lordship was sold to Jacques Ligier, treasurer general of the Cardinal de Bourbon, who built a chapel dedicated to the Holy Trinity.

Urbanization of the faubourg beyond the medieval abbey settlement began in 1622 with the subdivision of the former estate of Marguerite de Valois, Queen Margot, between the Seine, the rue de l'Université, and the rue du Bac. During the mid-seventeenth century, the southern section was occupied mainly by religious houses, including the Novitiate of the Dominicans in 1632, the Carmelite convent in 1656, and the Missions Étrangères in 1663.

Following the construction of the Pont Royal in 1685–1689 and the court's move to Versailles, aristocratic townhouses rapidly replaced the Marais as the city's most fashionable quarter.
